prompt.1: Ferries get cancelled, lines are long, and fares keep rising. What should the province change first?
prompt.2: BC Ferries has cancelled sailings, long waits and rising demand. Which change should the province push first?
prompt.3: BC Ferries has cancelled sailings, long waits, rising demand and a dispute over where ships are built. What should come first?
prompt.4: BC Ferries has cancellations, long waits and rising demand, and chose a Chinese state-owned yard for new ships. What comes first?
prompt.5: BC Ferries faces cancelled sailings, long waits and rising demand; in May 2025 it chose a Chinese state-owned shipyard for four hybrid vessels after no local yard bid. Which provincial change should come first?

context.1: Ferries are the only road for many Island and coast towns. Sailings get cancelled, waits are long, and fares keep rising. The province sets the ferry company's rules and money, and where new ships are built. Parties disagree on what to fix first.
context.2: BC Ferries is a provincially owned company that runs under rules and funding set by the province. Sailings get cancelled, waits are long and demand keeps rising. In 2025 the company ordered four new ships from a Chinese state-owned shipyard. In October four parties made ferry promises, none of them a fare cut. Parties disagree on what to fix first.
context.3: BC Ferries runs under a provincial mandate, with provincial funding and a provincially set board. Cancellations, long waits and rising demand are the common complaints. In May 2025 the company picked a Chinese state-owned yard for four hybrid-electric vessels after no local yard bid. On October 9 to 11 the Greens, the NDP and the Conservatives each announced ferry plans, and CentreBC's platform has two ferry items; none sets a new Swartz Bay schedule or cuts fares.
context.4: The province sets BC Ferries' mandate, service contract, funding and board rules. In May 2025 BC Ferries chose a Chinese state-owned shipyard for four large hybrid-electric vessels; the province says no local yard bid. The NDP announced a locals-first reservation pilot on October 10 (12% of advance booking space on two routes) and pledged in September that future vessels be built in BC. The Conservatives announced a BC Ferries Charter on October 11. The Greens released a ferry plan on October 9 and expanded it in their October 13 platform. CentreBC's platform has a shipyard fund and a fare credit. None of these sets a new Swartz Bay-Tsawwassen schedule or a fare cut.
context.5: The province sets BC Ferries' mandate, funding and board rules. In May 2025 BC Ferries selected a Chinese state-owned shipyard for four hybrid-electric vessels; the province says no Canadian yard bid. On September 18 Eby committed that future vessels be built in BC, with no timeline. On October 10 the NDP proposed a locals-first reservation pilot: 12% of advance booking space for residents of ferry-dependent communities, on Horseshoe Bay to Langdale and Westview to Little River only. On October 11 the Conservatives announced a BC Ferries Charter with service standards, board cuts and a federal 'fair share'. On October 9 the Greens proposed federal funding parity with Atlantic Canada, a governance review, electric ferries and locally built ships; their October 13 platform adds more vessels and restored Ferry Advisory Committees. CentreBC's platform offers Canadian-built vessels, a $25 million a year shipyard fund and a refundable 15% credit on multi-trip fares.

prompt.1: Island mills are closing, and people disagree about cutting the oldest forests. What should happen?
prompt.2: The Crofton pulp mill closed and old-growth logging is still argued over on the Island. What should the province do about forests?
prompt.3: The Crofton pulp mill has closed, and old-growth logging is still argued over on the Island. What should be done with Island forests?
prompt.4: Crofton's pulp mill has closed; old-growth deferrals remain, with a 45 million cubic metre harvest goal. What now?
prompt.5: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement, and Eby said pulping old growth to extend it was not an option; old-growth deferrals remain temporary. What now?

context.1: Logging has long been a big employer on the Island and the coast. A pulp mill near Duncan has closed. Some of the oldest forests are off limits for now. Parties disagree on protecting versus cutting.
context.2: The Crofton pulp mill, with about 350 jobs, closed last December. The premier said limits on old-growth logging were necessary and refused to let old growth be pulped to keep the mill open. Some old forests are under temporary logging deferrals. Parties disagree on what to protect and how much to cut.
context.3: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement. Eby said old-growth limits had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. Old-growth deferrals from 2021 are temporary. The government's Working Forest plan would zone forests with a 45 million cubic metre goal. The Greens reject the plan; CentreBC would write it into law.
context.4: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill closed after a December 2025 announcement; Eby said old-growth restrictions had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. Old-growth deferrals from 2021 remain temporary. The Forests minister's mandate letter sets a 45 million cubic metre harvest target while Budget 2026 projects about 30 million. On October 10 in Courtenay the NDP pledged $50 million to make the rarest deferrals permanent and help mills retrofit. The Greens would protect big-treed old growth permanently. CentreBC would legislate Working Forest zones. OneBC would raise the cut. The Conservatives would set a 45 million floor and protect only original old growth and the rarest ecosystems.
context.5: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill in the Cowichan Valley (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement; Eby said restrictions on old-growth harvesting had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. The 2021 old-growth deferrals remain temporary. Minister Parmar's mandate letter sets a 45 million cubic metre target; Budget 2026 projects about 30 million; the Working Forest model's first candidate area near Campbell River was announced September 15, 2026. On October 10 in Courtenay the NDP pledged $50 million to convert deferrals of 'the most irreplaceable and rarest forests' to permanent protection, with mill retrofit support for second growth. The Greens (October 4) would implement all 14 Old Growth Strategic Review recommendations and reject the 45 million target.

prompt.1: Island hospitals are short of space and seniors wait for care homes. What should come first?
prompt.2: Nanaimo's new hospital tower has planning money but no construction money, and care-home projects were paused. What should come first for seniors' care?
prompt.3: Nanaimo's hospital tower and cardiac lab are funded for planning, not construction, and a Campbell River care home was paused. What should come first?
prompt.4: Budget 2026 funded planning, not construction, for Nanaimo's tower and paused a 153-bed Campbell River care home. What should come first?
prompt.5: Budget 2026 funded concept planning, not construction, for Nanaimo's tower and cath lab, paused a 153-bed Campbell River care home, and about 1,600 patients province-wide wait in hospital for care beds. Which approach?

context.1: The Island has the oldest population in the province. Nanaimo has waited years for a bigger hospital. A care home in Campbell River was put on hold, and seniors wait in hospital beds for a care home place. Parties disagree on what to build first.
context.2: The government promised Nanaimo a new hospital tower and heart lab in 2024, but the 2026 budget paid only for planning. The same budget paused seven care-home projects, including a 153-bed home in Campbell River. In October the government promised to restart them. Parties disagree on what comes first.
context.3: The NDP's 2024 pledge of a tower and cardiac lab at Nanaimo's hospital got only planning money in Budget 2026. The same budget paused seven long-term care builds, including a 153-bed facility in Campbell River. In October the NDP promised to restart the seven and put $90 million into a campus of care at the former Oak Bay Lodge. The Conservatives would let care funding follow seniors to qualified providers, including non-government ones; CentreBC would cut seniors stuck in hospital.
context.4: The NDP's 2024 pledge of a patient tower and cardiac catheterization lab at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital was absent from the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds only initial planning. Budget 2026 also paused seven long-term care builds including a 153-bed Campbell River facility. The NDP (October 5 to 6) would restart the seven and spend $90 million on an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care. The Conservatives (October 9) would give waiting seniors portable public funding with a choice of qualified providers, including non-government ones. CentreBC would cut patients stuck in hospital awaiting care from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030. No party has a 2026 commitment on the Nanaimo tower.
context.5: The NDP's 2024 pledge of a patient tower and cardiac catheterization lab at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital was not in the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds initial planning only, the ministry says concept planning takes up to 18 months, and the Nanaimo Regional Hospital District agreed to put $50 million up front for concept and business planning of the cath lab. Budget 2026 paused seven long-term care projects including a 153-bed Campbell River facility, while the province looks for ways to cut building costs. The NDP pledges to restart the seven, $90 million toward an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care, scanners and rural recruitment incentives. The Conservatives (October 9) would give waiting seniors portable public funding with a choice of qualified providers, including non-government ones, and cut design rules. CentreBC would cut patients awaiting long-term care in hospital from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030. The Greens want community health centres and public-only funding.

scoring_rationale: No party has a 2026 commitment on the Nanaimo tower, so the question scores the seniors' care and hospital capacity approaches each party has published. a = NDP (4): restart the seven, Oak Bay Lodge, scanners, continued Nanaimo planning; CentreBC 3 (restarts the same seven and keeps care public, with its own design and targets); Green 2 (public expansion, no project pledge); Conservative 1 (builds the shelved beds through portable funding and non-government providers); OneBC 0. b = Conservative (4); OneBC 3 (private providers welcome, no portable funding or rural fund pledge); CentreBC 2 (rural fund overlaps, rejects non-government portable funding); NDP 1 (rural incentives only); Green 0. c = CentreBC (4); NDP 3 (same projects and public delivery, no stuck-patient target or accountability law); Conservative 3 (its October 18 platform restarts the same seven homes on a cheaper design and has a rural fund; rejects public-only delivery and has no stuck-patient target; score changed Oct 18 after the Conservative platform); Green 2 (public delivery overlaps); OneBC 1. d = Green (4); NDP 2 and CentreBC 2 (team clinics and public delivery, no ratios or single authority); Conservative 0; OneBC 0. e = OneBC (4), inferred from its private-care stance; Conservative 2 (non-government providers, public funding); others 0. The Interior's long-term care question uses the same party mapping with Okanagan projects; no voter sees both.
